new_statements.quote: General Rules. 1. When a word is unaccented, and contains more than one syllable, greater stress should be put on the first than on any of the others,— thus, "chuna," "now." Exceptions— (a)— Verbs in conjugation have, as a rule, the stress placed on the last syllable, e.g., "tagu," "will go." (b)— Adjectives when used with verbal terminations follow the above rule, and take the accent on the last syllable, thus "ida," "is good." 2. In compound words of three or more syllables, the lesser accent rests on the first and the greater on the middle, e.g., "Hai'gam"bau" (Naga proper name). [vowel diacritics in the examples are not reliably rendered by scanned]

new_statements.rule_in_words: In a polysyllabic word with no marked accent the first syllable carries the main stress. Verbs (and adjectives used predicatively with verbal endings) are stressed on the final conjugational suffix; in compounds of three or more syllables the main accent falls on the middle syllable with a lesser accent on the first; the interrogative particle -me and the iterative infix -dai- attract the main accent; disyllabic nouns move the accent to the second syllable when case suffixes are added, trisyllabic nouns do not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Soppitt marks a 'greater' (") and a 'lesser' (') accent; in compounds of three or more syllables the lesser accent is on the first syllable and the greater on the middle (§3 rule 2); in 'ta'dai'-gu-me"' both lesser and greater accents are shown.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs in conjugation and adjectives with verbal terminations: last syllable. Interrogative particle -me 'almost invariably takes the greater accent'. Iterative 'dai' between root and termination takes the stress. Dissyllabic nouns transfer the accent from the first to the second syllable when case-endings are affixed (mi'na -> mina'-ki), trisyllabic nouns do not (rule 5). Grierson 1903 (LSI III.2 p. 412), summarising Soppitt, restates the default as 'usually on the penultimate syllable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms and inflected forms), an impressionistic 1885 colonial outline grammar of 'Kachcha Naga (Empeo)' of the North Cachar Hills, i.e. Zeme (Glottolog files it under zeme1240). All three modern primary descriptions (Raguibou 2015 p. 48; Chanu 2017 p. 18; Muchahary 2019 p. 65) analyse Zeme as a lexical tone language (three tones high/mid/low or rising/level/falling; Chanu: two tones rising/falling) and contain no statement about word stress at all; Soppitt's 'accents' may partly reflect tone rather than stress. Treat as historical; no modern instrumental or phonological statement on stress exists in the sources examined.
new_statements.identity_note: Soppitt 1885 and Grierson 1903 describe 'Kachcha Naga / Empeo (Arung, Sengima, Jeme)' of the North Cachar Hills (now Dima Hasao, Assam); Grierson p. 411 says Jeme/Zeme is the general name of the tribe there and lists Inzemi, Sengima and Yema/Jema as its dialects; Glottolog files Soppitt under zeme1240. The modern theses describe Zeme of Manipur (Chanu 2017: Tousem sub-division, Tamenglong district) and Zeme Naga generally (Muchahary 2019; Raguibou 2015), all under nzm/zeme1240.

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology (pp. 16-57) has no stress/accent section and the word 'stress' does not occur; §3.2 Tone p. 18: 'Like many other Tibeto-Burman languages, Zeme has two tones i.e., raising and falling'; abstract: 'Zeme is a tonal language in which a change in the pitch of the syllable corresponds to a change in its meaning. Zeme has two tones namely (i) rising and (ii) falling.' Text layer garbled; scanned with tesseract at 300 dpi.

sources.note: p. 412 'Pronunciation': 'The accent is usually on the penultimate syllable, but in the case of conjugation is usually on the conjugational suffix. In interrogative sentences, it is on the interrogative suffix mé. There are numerous exceptions, which must be learned from Mr. Soppitt's Grammar.' Explicitly compiled second-hand from Soppitt 1885 (no specimens obtained).

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology (pp. 23-73): sections on vowels, consonants, syllable structure (§3.5), gemination, tone (§3.7) and morphophonemics; no stress/accent section, word 'stress' absent. §3.7 p. 65: 'Zeme is a tonal language with contrasting lexical elements. There are three tones in Zeme Naga i.e. rising, level and falling.' Ch. 1 §1.16 p. 11 repeats 'Zeme is a tonal language. It has three distinctive tones'.

sources.citation: Raguibou, I. D. 2015. The comparative phonology of Zeme, Liangmai and Rongmei. PhD thesis, Assam University, Silchar (supervisor Kh. Dhiren Singha). 159 pp.
sources.note: Ch. 3 'Overview of Zeme, Liangmai and Rongmei', §3.1 Zeme: syllable (C1)V1(V2)(C2)T with T = tone; §3.1.7 Tone p. 48: 'There are three contrastive tones in Zeme. They are high, mid (unmark) and low.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the chapter (scanned, 93 pp.).
States 'Like other Tibeto-Burman languages, Zeme is a tonal language', citing Chanu 2016/2017; nothing on stress.
